newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO to present military plan in 10 days.
newsitem.headline: NATO to present military plan in 10 days.

text.p: NATO will present detailed plans within the next 10 days to commit thousands of troops to Bosnia next year after non-alliance countries on Friday backed plans to keep the current multinational peace coalition together.
NATO sources said 18 non-NATO countries participating in the current Implementation Force (IFOR), whose mandate runs out in December, had expressed no objections to staying on in a new mission.
The 58,000-strong IFOR mission was sent to Bosnia to oversee the implementation of the Dayton peace accords which ended the 3 1/2-year Bosnia war.

NATO countries, edging towards a new commitment, instructed the military on Wednesday to start work on a possible new peace force, expected to number several thousand but below the current force level of some 58,000.

But first the alliance, keen to keep together the biggest coalition of countries seen in Europe since the Napoleonic era, opted to run various options past the non-NATO contributing members before presenting any proposals for a new force.
"I think everybody is extremely satisfied, the partners were fully briefed on the political-military guidelines and given the opportunity of comments," one NATO official said.
When IFOR was sent to Bosnia last December to police the Dayton accords, non-alliance countries were not consulted until after the planning stage was completed.
"This year we wanted to bring them in earlier," the official added.
Planning for a new force has unofficially been under way for months, but the issue is highly sensitive ahead of the U.S. presidential election on November 5.

NATO diplomats say Washington accepts the U.S. will have to commit ground troops to any new force or they will wreck the current alliance, which only emerged after years of transatlantic squabbling over how to deal with the Balkan crisis.

France and Britain, with memories of the ill-fated U.N. mission in Bosnia in which American ground forces were not involved, have said they would not stay on if the U.S. did not also keep troops in the country.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Thursday France and Germany had made advanced preparations for a joint peacekeeping force as part of any new mission.

A Franco-German brigade based in southwestern Germany had been earmarked for the job which would involve the first use of German troops in a potential combat role outside the NATO area since the end of World War Two.
NATO officials stressed no decision on replacing IFOR had yet been taken. Foreign and defence ministers will have to give approval after digesting the military's recommendations.
The military have been told to report back on how many troops would be needed to implement any of the following four options:
-- total withdrawal of the existing force in line with present political instructions
-- a deterrence force limited to preventing a fresh outbreak of fighting
-- a deterrence force with a mandate to increase stability and to give limited help to civilian reconstruction efforts
-- a deterrence force with a mandate to increase stability and give wide-ranging support to civilian reconstruction efforts.
